## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Functional Brain Imaging and Brain–Computer Interfaces
  Official title       Imagerie fonctionnelle cérébrale et interface cerveau machine
  Instructors          B. THIRION, M.C. CORSI (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 2 · period 2 (04/01/2027 – 02/04/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 24 h (lectures 24 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Modelling]{.badge .label}[Track Santé]{.badge .track}
  Language             Not displayed; the course description on master-mva.com is written in French
  Assessment           Two TDs (“L’évaluation du cours est constituée de 2 TD”, master-mva.com, “Mode de validation”); the resit is a critical commentary of a research paper; no weighting is displayed; the Université Paris-Saclay course detail gives the nature of the assessment as “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale”
  Prerequisites        Integral calculus, elements of statistics, numerical computation, linear algebra, optimization (master-mva.com, “Prè-requis”)
  -------------------- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with a good M1 in mathematics, computer science or physics who wants to turn the electromagnetic or haemodynamic traces of brain activity into maps, statistics and commands, whether for neuroscience, for the clinic or for a brain–computer interface.

**Empirical first**: Bennett and colleagues put a dead Atlantic salmon in an MRI scanner, "showed" it photographs of people in social situations, and thresholded the voxelwise statistics at an uncorrected $p < 0.001$: a few voxels in the fish's brain came out "active". Years later, Eklund, Nichols and Knutsson (2016) ran standard group analyses on resting-state data, where no task effect exists. Parametric cluster inference gave familywise false-positive rates far above the nominal 5%. Both failures come from statistics ([ch. 6](#ch6)), not from the scanner.

The course is about two non-invasive windows on the working brain. Magneto- and electroencephalography (M/EEG) record, within milliseconds, the fields created by currents in the cortex. Functional MRI records, within millimetres but over seconds, a haemodynamic signal tied to the energy used by brain areas.

The page follows the official syllabus: the physics of the signals, the forward and inverse problems of M/EEG, the statistical analysis of functional images and networks, and brain–computer interfaces (BCIs). It shares the neural modelling of [Mathematical Methods for Neuroscience](../s1-neuroscience-maths/index.html), the regularised inversion of [Inverse Problems and Imaging](../s2-inverse-problems-imaging/index.html) and the clinical statistics of [Biostatistics](../s2-biostatistics/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Derive the quasistatic equations of bioelectromagnetism and compute the potential and magnetic field of a current dipole.
-   Explain why MEG is blind to radial sources in a spherical head, and prove it.
-   Write the M/EEG forward problem as a boundary value problem, solve it with finite elements, and build a lead field by reciprocity.
-   Denoise M/EEG recordings by filtering, averaging, whitening, signal-space projection and independent component analysis.
-   Localise sources with dipole fitting, MUSIC, beamformers and minimum-norm imaging, and validate them with resolution matrices and simulations.
-   Model an fMRI time series with the general linear model, test contrasts, and run a group analysis with mixed effects.
-   Control false positives in statistical maps with permutation tests, familywise and false discovery rate procedures, and cluster inference.
-   Estimate functional connectivity with partial correlations, shrinkage, the graphical lasso and the geometry of covariance matrices, and recognise the effect of volume conduction on M/EEG coherence.
-   Build and evaluate a BCI pipeline (common spatial patterns, linear discriminant analysis, Riemannian classifiers) without leakage, and compute its information transfer rate.
-   Discuss the role of feedback and user learning in a closed-loop BCI.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com states that the course deals with functional brain imaging and its application to brain–computer interfaces, based on two non-invasive techniques that measure brain activity. M/EEG measures the electromagnetic field created by cortical electric currents; functional MRI measures a signal (BOLD) linked to the energy consumption of brain areas.

### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisites: integral calculus, elements of statistics, numerical computation, linear algebra and optimization. The course is a second-semester Modelling course of 5 ECTS of the Santé track, taught by Bertrand Thirion and Marie-Constance Corsi (INRIA, as listed on master-mva.com).

-   **Refreshers** — [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) for the SVD, Tikhonov regularisation and the Lagrange multipliers of [ch. 0](#ch0) and [ch. 4](#ch4); [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) for the Gaussian linear model and the tests of [ch. 5](#ch5)–[ch. 6](#ch6); [Scientific Python, NumPy and PyTorch](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) for the code.
-   **First-semester courses that prepare it** — [Mathematical Methods for Neuroscience](../s1-neuroscience-maths/index.html) (where the currents come from); [Convex Optimization and Applications in Machine Learning](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html) (graphical lasso, proximal methods of section 9.2); [Introduction to Statistical Learning](../s1-intro-statistical-learning/index.html) (LDA, cross-validation); [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html) (resampling); [Machine Learning for Time Series](../s1-time-series/index.html) (filtering, spectra); [Medical Image Analysis Based on Generative, Geometric and Biophysical Models](../s1-medical-image-analysis/index.html) (MRI, registration, the Santé track).
-   **Related second-semester courses** — [Inverse Problems and Imaging](../s2-inverse-problems-imaging/index.html) (Bayesian regularisation); [Large Random Matrices and Applications to Machine Learning](../s2-random-matrices-ml/index.html) (covariance estimation in high dimension); [Biostatistics](../s2-biostatistics/index.html) (mixed models, clinical validation); [Deep Learning for Medical Imaging](../s2-deep-learning-medical-imaging/index.html); [Graphs in Machine Learning](../s2-graphs-in-ml/index.html) (brain networks as graphs); [Kernel Methods for Machine Learning](../s2-kernel-methods/index.html); [Audio Signal Processing: Time–Frequency Analysis](../s2-audio-time-frequency/index.html) (spectral estimation).
-   **Alongside and after the course** — the [Hospital Immersion: Paired Project with a Physician](../year-hospital-immersion/index.html), where clinical EEG and MRI are met in practice, and the [Research Internship](../s3-research-internship/index.html).

### Course outline

-   **Review: vector calculus, linear algebra and the Gaussian linear model** — divergence theorem and Green's identity, the fundamental solution of the Laplacian, SVD and Tikhonov regularisation, Rayleigh quotients, the distribution of least squares.
-   **From neural currents to electromagnetic fields** — the origin of M/EEG signals, the quasistatic Maxwell equations, the current dipole, Biot–Savart, spherical models and the silence of radial dipoles, source models.
-   **The M/EEG forward problem and finite elements** — the boundary value problem, its weak form, P1 finite elements, singular sources, the lead field and Helmholtz reciprocity.
-   **Preprocessing and denoising M/EEG signals** — filtering and averaging, noise covariance and whitening, signal-space projection, independent component analysis.
-   **The M/EEG inverse problem** — ill-posedness, dipole fitting, MUSIC, beamformers, minimum-norm imaging, dSPM and sLORETA, validation.
-   **fMRI: the BOLD signal and the general linear model** — the haemodynamic response, design matrices, contrasts, prewhitening, mixed-effects group models.
-   **Hypothesis testing and multiple comparisons** — permutation tests, familywise error rate, false discovery rate, cluster-level inference.
-   **Connectivity, networks and covariance learning** — partial correlations, shrinkage, the graphical lasso, the manifold of covariance matrices.
-   **Brain–computer interfaces** — paradigms, information transfer rate, common spatial patterns, linear and Riemannian classifiers, evaluation, feedback.
-   **Complements** — boundary elements and the Geselowitz formula, Maxwell filtering, sparse source imaging, random field theory, decoding and the interpretation of weights, M/EEG coherence and volume conduction, effective connectivity (self-study).
-   **Research directions and open problems** — reproducibility, large cohorts, deep decoding of non-invasive signals, transfer across sessions and subjects, user training (self-study).

### How to study this module

-   Read [ch. 0](#ch0) first, even quickly: Green's identity, the push-through identity and the distribution of least squares are used without warning in [ch. 2](#ch2), [ch. 4](#ch4) and [ch. 5](#ch5).
-   Keep the orders of magnitude of Example 1.3 and Example 1.6 in mind: they explain most modelling choices of the M/EEG chapters.
-   Run every code block: they use NumPy, SciPy and scikit-learn only, with fixed seeds and synthetic data, and each runs in a few seconds. Then change one parameter (the noise level, the depth of a source, the number of trials) and predict the output before running again.
-   After each session, solve the exercises of the *Practice* column; the ★★★ exercises are good starting points for a TD or a project.
-   For real data, the open-source libraries MNE-Python (M/EEG), Nilearn (fMRI) and pyRiemann (BCI) implement the methods of this page; the [projects](#projects) use them on public data sets.
-   Read [ch. 9](#ch9) section by section as the matching chapter is taught: 9.1 after session 3, 9.2 after session 5, 9.3 after session 7, 9.4–9.6 after session 8.

## 0. Review: vector calculus, linear algebra and the Gaussian linear model {#ch0}

Three M1 toolboxes are used: vector calculus for the physics of [ch. 1](#ch1)–[ch. 2](#ch2), regularised least squares for [ch. 4](#ch4), and the Gaussian linear model for [ch. 5](#ch5)–[ch. 6](#ch6). This chapter states them with short proofs.

### 0.1 Vector calculus

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Differential operators]{.tag} For a scalar field $f$ and a vector field $F$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$:
$$
\nabla f = (\partial_1 f, \partial_2 f, \partial_3 f), \qquad \nabla \cdot F = \sum_i \partial_i F_i, \qquad \nabla \times F = \big(\partial_2 F_3 - \partial_3 F_2,\ \partial_3 F_1 - \partial_1 F_3,\ \partial_1 F_2 - \partial_2 F_1\big),
$$
and $\Delta f = \nabla \cdot \nabla f$. Two identities hold for smooth fields:
$$
\nabla \times (\nabla f) = 0, \qquad \nabla \cdot (\nabla \times F) = 0 .
$$
Conversely, on a simply connected domain a curl-free field is a gradient.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.2 — Divergence theorem and Green's first identity]{.tag} Let $\Omega$ be a bounded domain with smooth boundary $\partial\Omega$ and outward normal $n$.

For smooth fields $F$, $u$, $w$ and a positive function $\sigma$:
$$
\int_\Omega \nabla \cdot F \, dr = \oint_{\partial\Omega} F \cdot n \, dS, \qquad \int_\Omega w\, \nabla \cdot (\sigma \nabla u)\, dr = \oint_{\partial\Omega} w\, \sigma\, \partial_n u \, dS - \int_\Omega \sigma\, \nabla u \cdot \nabla w \, dr .
$$

::: proof
The first formula is the Gauss–Ostrogradski theorem. The second applies it to $F = w\,\sigma \nabla u$, whose divergence is
$$
\nabla \cdot (w\,\sigma \nabla u) = w\, \nabla\cdot(\sigma\nabla u) + \sigma \nabla u \cdot \nabla w .
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 0.3 — Fundamental solution of the Laplacian]{.tag} In $\mathbb{R}^3$, in the sense of distributions,
$$
\Delta \Big( -\frac{1}{4\pi |r|} \Big) = \delta_0, \qquad \nabla_r \frac{1}{|r - r'|} = -\frac{r - r'}{|r - r'|^3} = -\nabla_{r'} \frac{1}{|r - r'|} .
$$
In $\mathbb{R}^2$ the fundamental solution is $\frac{1}{2\pi}\ln|r|$. The solution of $\Delta u = f$ that vanishes at infinity is the convolution of $f$ with the fundamental solution.
:::

### 0.2 Singular values and regularised least squares

::: def
[Definition 0.4 — SVD and pseudo-inverse]{.tag} Every $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times p}$ factors as $A = U \Sigma V^\top$ with $U$, $V$ orthogonal and $\Sigma$ diagonal with entries $s_1 \ge s_2 \ge \dots \ge 0$.

The pseudo-inverse is $A^+ = V \Sigma^+ U^\top$, where $\Sigma^+$ inverts the non-zero singular values. The vector $A^+ y$ is the least-squares solution of minimum norm.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.5 — Tikhonov regularisation and the push-through identity]{.tag} For $\lambda > 0$, the problem $\min_x \|y - Ax\|^2 + \lambda \|x\|^2$ has the unique solution
$$
\hat x_\lambda = (A^\top A + \lambda I_p)^{-1} A^\top y = A^\top (A A^\top + \lambda I_m)^{-1} y = \sum_i \frac{s_i}{s_i^2 + \lambda}\, (u_i^\top y)\, v_i .
$$

::: proof
The objective is strictly convex; its gradient $2A^\top(Ax - y) + 2\lambda x$ vanishes at the first expression.

The identity $A^\top (AA^\top + \lambda I) = (A^\top A + \lambda I) A^\top$ gives the second one after multiplication by both inverses.

The third follows by inserting the SVD: each component $u_i^\top y$ is divided by $s_i$ and damped by the filter factor $s_i^2/(s_i^2+\lambda)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The second form costs one $m \times m$ inversion. With $m \approx 300$ sensors and $p \approx 10^4$ sources, this is what makes minimum-norm imaging cheap ([ch. 4](#ch4)).

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.6 — Generalised Rayleigh quotient]{.tag} Let $C_1$ be symmetric and $C_2$ symmetric positive definite. The quotient
$$
R(w) = \frac{w^\top C_1 w}{w^\top C_2 w}
$$
is maximised (minimised) by the eigenvector of the generalised problem $C_1 w = \mu C_2 w$ with the largest (smallest) eigenvalue $\mu$, and the extreme values of $R$ are these eigenvalues.

::: proof
Set $v = C_2^{1/2} w$. Then $R = v^\top M v / v^\top v$ with $M = C_2^{-1/2} C_1 C_2^{-1/2}$ symmetric. The ordinary Rayleigh principle gives the extreme eigenvectors of $M$, and $M v = \mu v$ is equivalent to $C_1 w = \mu C_2 w$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 0.3 The Gaussian linear model

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.7 — Distribution of least squares]{.tag} Let $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$ with $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ of rank $p$ and $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I_n)$. Then $\hat\beta = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y$ and the residual variance $\hat\sigma^2 = \|y - X\hat\beta\|^2/(n-p)$ satisfy
$$
\hat\beta \sim \mathcal{N}\big(\beta, \sigma^2 (X^\top X)^{-1}\big), \qquad \frac{(n-p)\,\hat\sigma^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-p}, \qquad \hat\beta \perp \hat\sigma^2 .
$$

::: proof
$\hat\beta$ is a linear function of a Gaussian vector, with the stated mean and covariance. The residual is $(I - H)\varepsilon$, where $H = X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top$ is the orthogonal projector onto the columns of $X$.

Since $I - H$ is a projector of rank $n - p$, $\|(I-H)\varepsilon\|^2/\sigma^2$ is $\chi^2_{n-p}$ (Cochran).

Finally $\hat\beta$ depends on $H\varepsilon$ and the residual on $(I-H)\varepsilon$: these Gaussian vectors are uncorrelated, hence independent. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 0
:::

-   Green's identity turns a boundary value problem into an energy identity; it gives uniqueness in [ch. 2](#ch2) and reciprocity in section 2.4.
-   Tikhonov regularisation damps small singular values; its "sensor-space" form needs one $m \times m$ inversion.
-   Generalised eigenvectors maximise ratios of variances; they reappear in CSP ([ch. 8](#ch8)).
-   In the Gaussian linear model, $\hat\beta$ is Gaussian and independent of $\hat\sigma^2$, which yields the $t$ and $F$ tests of [ch. 5](#ch5).
::::

## 1. From neural currents to electromagnetic fields {#ch1}

This chapter follows the signal from the synapse to the sensor and reduces Maxwell's equations to the two formulas used by M/EEG software: a Poisson equation for the potential and the Biot–Savart law for the field.

### 1.1 Where the signals come from

When a neurotransmitter opens ion channels on the dendrite of a cortical pyramidal neuron, a current enters the cell, flows along the dendrite, and returns through the extracellular medium. The intracellular part of this loop is the **primary current**; the extracellular return is the **volume current**.

Pyramidal cells are aligned perpendicular to the cortical surface, so their primary currents add up when synchronous; a measurable signal needs tens of thousands of cells active together. Brief action potentials contribute little at a distance.

| | EEG | MEG | fMRI |
|---|---|---|---|
| Measures | potential differences on the scalp | magnetic field outside the head | BOLD signal (blood oxygenation) |
| Typical amplitude | 10–100 µV | 10–1000 fT | 1–5 % signal change |
| Temporal resolution | about 1 ms | about 1 ms | seconds (sampling every 1–2 s) |
| Spatial resolution | centimetres, after source modelling | centimetres to millimetres, after source modelling | 2–3 mm voxels |
| Sensors | 32–256 electrodes | about 300 sensors in a shielded room | MRI scanner |

The magnetic field of the brain is about $10^8$ times smaller than the Earth's field of 50 µT; MEG needs superconducting or optically pumped magnetometers in a magnetically shielded room.

### 1.2 Maxwell's equations in the quasistatic regime

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Maxwell's equations in a conductor]{.tag} In a medium of conductivity $\sigma$, permittivity $\varepsilon$ and permeability $\mu_0$, the fields $E$, $B$ and the current density $J$ satisfy
$$
\nabla \cdot E = \frac{\rho}{\varepsilon}, \qquad \nabla \times E = -\partial_t B, \qquad \nabla \cdot B = 0, \qquad \nabla \times B = \mu_0 \big( J + \varepsilon\, \partial_t E \big).
$$
The total current is the sum of the primary current and the ohmic volume current:
$$
J = J^p + \sigma E .
$$
:::

Brain signals lie below about 1 kHz. Two dimensionless numbers then justify dropping the time derivatives: the ratio of displacement to ohmic currents, $\omega\varepsilon/\sigma$, and the ratio of the head size to the skin depth $\delta = \sqrt{2/(\omega \mu_0 \sigma)}$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.2 — Quasistatic equations]{.tag} If $\partial_t B$ and $\varepsilon\,\partial_t E$ are neglected, the electric field derives from a potential, $E = -\nabla V$, and $V$ solves the Poisson equation

::: key
[Key result — the M/EEG forward equation]{.tag}
$$
\nabla \cdot (\sigma \nabla V) = \nabla \cdot J^p
$$
:::

::: proof
Without $\partial_t B$, $\nabla \times E = 0$, so $E = -\nabla V$ (Definition 0.1).

Without $\varepsilon\,\partial_t E$, $\nabla \times B = \mu_0 J$; taking the divergence gives $\nabla \cdot J = 0$.

Substituting $J = J^p - \sigma \nabla V$ yields the equation. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The time dependence is now a parameter: at every instant the potential is the static response to the primary currents of that instant. This is why M/EEG models are linear and instantaneous.

::: ex
[Example 1.3 — Orders of magnitude]{.tag} Take $\sigma = 0.33$ S/m (brain and scalp) and a frequency of 100 Hz, so $\omega = 628$ rad/s.

-   Even with a large relative permittivity of $10^5$, the ratio of displacement to ohmic currents is
    $$
    \frac{\omega \varepsilon}{\sigma} = \frac{628 \times 10^5 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12}}{0.33} \approx 1.7 \times 10^{-3} .
    $$
-   The skin depth is
    $$
    \delta = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\omega \mu_0 \sigma}} \approx 88 \text{ m},
    $$
    about a thousand times the size of a head, so induction is negligible.
-   At 1 kHz the two numbers become $1.7 \times 10^{-2}$ and 28 m: the approximation still holds.
:::

### 1.3 The current dipole and the potential in a homogeneous medium

::: def
[Definition 1.4 — Current dipole]{.tag} A primary current concentrated at $r_0$ with moment $q \in \mathbb{R}^3$ (unit A·m) is the **current dipole**
$$
J^p(r) = q\, \delta(r - r_0) .
$$
A synchronously active patch of cortex of a few square millimetres is well summarised by a dipole of 1–100 nA·m, oriented along the normal to the cortex.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.5 — Potential of a dipole in an infinite homogeneous conductor]{.tag} If $\sigma$ is constant on $\mathbb{R}^3$, the solution of Proposition 1.2 that vanishes at infinity is
$$
V_\infty(r) = \frac{1}{4\pi\sigma}\, \frac{q \cdot (r - r_0)}{|r - r_0|^3} .
$$

::: proof
The equation reads $\Delta V = \nabla \cdot J^p / \sigma$. By Proposition 0.3,
$$
V(r) = -\frac{1}{4\pi\sigma} \int \frac{\nabla' \cdot J^p(r')}{|r - r'|}\, dr' = \frac{1}{4\pi\sigma} \int J^p(r') \cdot \nabla' \frac{1}{|r - r'|}\, dr',
$$
after an integration by parts. With $\nabla' |r - r'|^{-1} = (r - r')/|r - r'|^3$ and $J^p = q\,\delta_{r_0}$, the integral evaluates at $r' = r_0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The potential decreases as the inverse square of the distance, with a positive lobe in the direction of $q$ and a negative lobe behind it.

::: ex
[Example 1.6 — An evoked source seen from 4 cm]{.tag} A dipole of $q = 10$ nA·m in $\sigma = 0.33$ S/m, observed at 4 cm along its axis, produces
$$
V_\infty = \frac{10^{-8}}{4\pi \times 0.33 \times 0.04^2} \approx 1.5 \ \mu\text{V}.
$$
The poorly conducting skull, between about 15 and 80 times less conductive than the brain depending on the study, smears this potential over the scalp. This is why the head must be modelled ([ch. 2](#ch2)).
:::

### 1.4 The magnetic field: Biot–Savart

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.7 — Biot–Savart law]{.tag} Under the quasistatic approximation, $\nabla \times B = \mu_0 J$ and $\nabla \cdot B = 0$ give, for currents of bounded support,
$$
B(r) = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \int J(r') \times \frac{r - r'}{|r - r'|^3}\, dr' .
$$

::: proof
Since $\nabla\cdot B = 0$, write $B = \nabla \times A$ with the gauge $\nabla \cdot A = 0$. Then
$$
\nabla \times \nabla \times A = \nabla(\nabla\cdot A) - \Delta A = -\Delta A = \mu_0 J .
$$
Proposition 0.3 gives $A(r) = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int J(r')/|r - r'|\, dr'$. Taking the curl under the integral, with $\nabla_r |r - r'|^{-1} = -(r - r')/|r - r'|^3$, gives the formula. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Both primary and volume currents contribute. Splitting $J = J^p - \sigma \nabla V$ gives $B = B_0 + B_v$, where $B_0$ is the field of the primary current alone.

::: prop
[Proposition 1.8 — Field of the primary dipole]{.tag} For $J^p = q\,\delta_{r_0}$,
$$
B_0(r) = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\, \frac{q \times (r - r_0)}{|r - r_0|^3} .
$$
For $q = 10$ nA·m at 4 cm, perpendicular to $q$, this gives $10^{-7} \times 10^{-8}/0.04^2 \approx 625$ fT, the order of magnitude of evoked MEG responses.
:::

### 1.5 Spherical head models

In general the volume currents depend on the whole conductivity profile. A sphere is the exception that makes MEG modelling simple.

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.9 — MEG in a spherically symmetric conductor]{.tag} Let the conductivity depend only on $|r|$ inside a ball and vanish outside. For every $r$ outside the ball:

1.  the volume currents do not contribute to the radial component, $r \cdot B(r) = r \cdot B_0(r)$;
2.  the field $B$ outside depends only on $q$ and $r_0$, not on the conductivity profile;
3.  a radial dipole ($q$ parallel to $r_0$) produces no magnetic field outside the ball.

::: proof
*Step 1.* The volume currents contribute
$$
B_v(r) = -\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int \sigma(r')\,\nabla' V \times \frac{r - r'}{|r - r'|^3}\, dr' .
$$
Using $(a \times b)\cdot c = a \cdot (b \times c)$,
$$
\Big(\nabla' V \times (r - r')\Big) \cdot r = \nabla' V \cdot \big((r - r') \times r\big) = \nabla' V \cdot (r \times r') .
$$
Integrate by parts, moving the gradient onto
$$
f(r') = \sigma(|r'|)\, \frac{r \times r'}{|r - r'|^3} .
$$
Three terms appear, and all vanish:

-   the divergence of $r \times r'$ in $r'$ is zero;
-   the gradient of $\sigma(|r'|)$, including the jump at the surface, is parallel to $r'$, which is orthogonal to $r \times r'$;
-   the gradient of $|r - r'|^{-3}$ is parallel to $r - r'$, also orthogonal to $r \times r'$.

*Step 2.* Outside the conductor $J = 0$, so $\nabla \times B = 0$ and $B = -\mu_0 \nabla U$, with $U \to 0$ at infinity. Integrating along the ray from $r$ to infinity,
$$
U(r) = \frac{1}{\mu_0} \int_0^\infty \hat r \cdot B(r + t \hat r)\, dt ,
$$
which, by step 1, only involves $B_0$, hence only $q$ and $r_0$.

*Step 3.* Expand the radial part of the primary field:
$$
r \cdot \big(q \times (r - r_0)\big) = r \cdot (q \times r) - r \cdot (q \times r_0) = -\, r \cdot (q \times r_0) .
$$
If $q$ is parallel to $r_0$, then $q \times r_0 = 0$, so $r \cdot B_0 = 0$ everywhere outside. By step 2, $U = 0$ and $B = 0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

MEG is thus blind to radial sources, located at the crests of the gyri, and most sensitive to tangential sources in the walls of the sulci. EEG sees both, which is one reason to combine the two modalities.

::: prop
[Proposition 1.10 — Sarvas formula (Sarvas, 1987)]{.tag} With the sphere centred at 0, $a = r - r_0$, $a = |a|$ and $r = |r|$, the field outside is
$$
B(r) = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi F^2}\Big( F\, q \times r_0 - \big((q \times r_0)\cdot r\big)\, \nabla F \Big), \qquad F = a\,(r a + r^2 - r_0 \cdot r),
$$
$$
\nabla F = \Big(\frac{a^2}{r} + \frac{a \cdot r}{a} + 2a + 2r\Big)\, r - \Big(a + 2r + \frac{a \cdot r}{a}\Big)\, r_0 .
$$
It is obtained by computing the integral of step 2 in closed form. It depends on $q$ only through $q \times r_0$: the radial part of $q$ drops out.
:::

::: ex
[Code 1.11 — Sarvas field, primary field and the silent radial dipole]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np

mu0 = 4e-7 * np.pi

def b_primary(r, r0, q):
    """Biot-Savart field of the primary current dipole alone (T)."""
    a = r - r0
    return mu0 / (4 * np.pi) * np.cross(q, a) / np.linalg.norm(a) ** 3

def b_sarvas(r, r0, q):
    """Field outside a spherically symmetric conductor centred at 0 (Sarvas, 1987)."""
    a_vec = r - r0
    a, rn = np.linalg.norm(a_vec), np.linalg.norm(r)
    F = a * (rn * a + rn**2 - r0 @ r)
    gradF = ((a**2 / rn + a_vec @ r / a + 2 * a + 2 * rn) * r
             - (a + 2 * rn + a_vec @ r / a) * r0)
    qxr0 = np.cross(q, r0)
    return mu0 / (4 * np.pi * F**2) * (F * qxr0 - (qxr0 @ r) * gradF)

r0 = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.07])           # source 7 cm from the centre
r = np.array([0.03, 0.01, 0.105])         # sensor about 4 cm away
rhat = r / np.linalg.norm(r)
q_tan = np.array([10e-9, 0.0, 0.0])       # 10 nAm tangential dipole
q_rad = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 10e-9])       # 10 nAm radial dipole

for name, q in [("tangential", q_tan), ("radial", q_rad)]:
    B, B0 = b_sarvas(r, r0, q), b_primary(r, r0, q)
    print(f"{name:10s} |B| = {np.linalg.norm(B)*1e15:7.1f} fT, |B0| = "
          f"{np.linalg.norm(B0)*1e15:7.1f} fT, radial parts: "
          f"{B @ rhat*1e15:7.2f} vs {B0 @ rhat*1e15:7.2f} fT")
```

Output: the tangential dipole gives $|B| = 156.9$ fT against $|B_0| = 346.8$ fT, with equal radial parts of 60.82 fT (Theorem 1.9). The radial dipole gives $|B| = 0$: volume currents cancel its 301 fT primary field.
:::

### 1.6 Source models

::: def
[Definition 1.12 — Source models and lead field]{.tag} By linearity of Proposition 1.2 in $J^p$, the measurements are linear in the dipole moments. Three source models are used:

-   **Equivalent current dipoles**: a few dipoles with unknown positions $r_k$ and moments $q_k$; the model is nonlinear in $r_k$.
-   **Distributed models**: $p$ dipoles at fixed positions on a grid or on the cortical surface, with unknown moments; the model is linear.
-   **Orientation constraints**: a free orientation uses three unknowns per position; a fixed orientation, normal to the cortical surface extracted from an anatomical MRI, uses one.

For $m$ sensors and a distributed model, the **lead field** (gain matrix) $G \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times p}$ maps source amplitudes to measurements: $M = G J + N$.
:::

Column $j$ of $G$ is the topography that a unit source at position $j$ would produce on the sensors. Computing it is the forward problem of [ch. 2](#ch2); inverting it is the inverse problem of [ch. 4](#ch4).

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 1
:::

-   M/EEG signals come from synchronous postsynaptic currents of pyramidal neurons; a 10 nA·m dipole gives about a microvolt and a few hundred femtotesla.
-   Below 1 kHz the quasistatic approximation holds: $\nabla\cdot(\sigma\nabla V) = \nabla\cdot J^p$, and $B$ follows from Biot–Savart.
-   The measurements are linear in the source moments; positions enter nonlinearly.
-   In a spherical conductor, the external magnetic field depends only on $q \times r_0$: MEG is blind to radial dipoles, whatever the conductivity profile.
::::

## 2. The M/EEG forward problem and finite elements {#ch2}

Given a source, what do the sensors of a realistic head record? This **forward problem** is a boundary value problem; this chapter solves it with finite elements and uses reciprocity to get a whole lead field from one solve per electrode.

### 2.1 The boundary value problem

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — The EEG forward problem]{.tag} Let $\Omega$ be the head, a bounded domain with outward normal $n$, and $\sigma$ its conductivity, piecewise constant or tensor-valued. Given a primary current $J^p$ supported inside $\Omega$, find $V$ such that
$$
\nabla \cdot (\sigma \nabla V) = \nabla \cdot J^p \ \text{ in } \Omega, \qquad \sigma\, \partial_n V = 0 \ \text{ on } \partial\Omega .
$$
The boundary condition says that no current flows into the air. Across internal interfaces, $V$ and the normal current $\sigma\,\partial_n V$ are continuous.
:::

Typical values are about 0.33 S/m for the scalp and the grey matter, 1.79 S/m for the cerebrospinal fluid, and between 0.004 and 0.02 S/m for the skull; the white matter is anisotropic. The skull value is the main source of modelling error in EEG.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — Compatibility and uniqueness]{.tag} The data of Definition 2.1 are compatible, and two solutions differ by a constant on a connected $\Omega$.

::: proof
*Compatibility.* By the divergence theorem and the boundary condition,
$$
\int_\Omega \nabla\cdot(\sigma\nabla V) = \oint \sigma\,\partial_n V = 0 .
$$
Likewise $\int_\Omega \nabla \cdot J^p = \oint J^p \cdot n = 0$, since $J^p$ vanishes near the boundary.

*Uniqueness.* The difference $W$ of two solutions satisfies the homogeneous problem. Green's identity (Theorem 0.2) with $u = w = W$ gives
$$
\int_\Omega \sigma\, |\nabla W|^2 = 0,
$$
so $\nabla W = 0$ and $W$ is constant. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The potential is only defined up to a constant: EEG always measures differences, with respect to a reference electrode or to the average of all electrodes.

### 2.2 Weak formulation

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.3 — Variational formulation and well-posedness]{.tag} Let $0 < \sigma_{\min} \le \sigma \le \sigma_{\max}$ and $J^p \in L^2(\Omega)^3$. Let $H$ be the space of functions of $H^1(\Omega)$ with zero mean. There is a unique $V \in H$ such that
$$
a(V, w) := \int_\Omega \sigma\, \nabla V \cdot \nabla w \, dr = \int_\Omega J^p \cdot \nabla w \, dr =: \ell(w) \qquad \text{for all } w \in H^1(\Omega).
$$

::: proof
*From strong to weak.* Multiply the equation by $w$ and apply Green's identity on both sides. The boundary term on the left vanishes by the Neumann condition, and the one on the right because $J^p = 0$ on $\partial\Omega$.

*Well-posedness.* For constant $w$ both sides vanish, so testing on $H$ suffices. The form $a$ is continuous on $H^1$. On $H$, the Poincaré–Wirtinger inequality $\|w\|_{L^2} \le C_P \|\nabla w\|_{L^2}$ makes it coercive:
$$
a(w, w) \ge \sigma_{\min} \|\nabla w\|^2 \ge \frac{\sigma_{\min}}{1 + C_P^2}\, \|w\|_{H^1}^2 .
$$
Since $\ell$ is continuous, the Lax–Milgram theorem concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A point dipole is not in $L^2$: for it, $\ell(w) = q \cdot \nabla w(r_0)$, which is not continuous on $H^1$. Two classical remedies follow. The *direct* approach evaluates this formula on piecewise-linear test functions anyway. The *subtraction* approach removes the singularity analytically (Proposition 2.6).

### 2.3 Galerkin approximation with P1 elements

::: def
[Definition 2.4 — P1 finite elements]{.tag} Mesh $\Omega$ into tetrahedra (triangles in 2D) of size $h$, with nodes $x_1, \dots, x_N$. Let $\varphi_i$ be the continuous, piecewise-linear "hat" function with $\varphi_i(x_j) = \delta_{ij}$.

Seeking $V_h = \sum_j v_j \varphi_j$ with $a(V_h, \varphi_i) = \ell(\varphi_i)$ for all $i$ gives the linear system
$$
K v = b, \qquad K_{ij} = \int_\Omega \sigma\, \nabla \varphi_i \cdot \nabla \varphi_j, \qquad b_i = \ell(\varphi_i) .
$$
$K$ is sparse, symmetric and positive semi-definite, with kernel spanned by the constant vector. For a dipole, the direct approach takes $b_i = q \cdot \nabla \varphi_i(r_0)$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.5 — Céa's lemma (energy-norm optimality)]{.tag} Let $V$ solve Theorem 2.3 and $V_h$ the Galerkin problem, both with zero mean, and write $\|u\|_a^2 = a(u, u)$. Then $V_h$ is the best approximation of $V$ in the discrete space:
$$
\|V - V_h\|_a = \min_{w_h} \|V - w_h\|_a .
$$

::: proof
Subtracting the discrete equations from the continuous ones gives *Galerkin orthogonality*: $a(V - V_h, w_h) = 0$ for every discrete $w_h$.

For any $w_h$, write $V - w_h = (V - V_h) + (V_h - w_h)$, with the second term discrete. By orthogonality,
$$
\|V - w_h\|_a^2 = \|V - V_h\|_a^2 + \|V_h - w_h\|_a^2 \ge \|V - V_h\|_a^2 .
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For a smooth solution, interpolation gives an error of order $h$ in the energy norm and $h^2$ in $L^2$ (Ern and Guermond, 2004). A dipole solution is not smooth near $r_0$, which spoils this rate unless the singularity is removed.

::: prop
[Proposition 2.6 — Subtraction source model]{.tag} Suppose $\sigma$ equals a constant $\sigma_\infty$ near $r_0$, and let $V_\infty$ be the infinite-medium potential of Proposition 1.5 computed with $\sigma_\infty$.

Then $V = V_\infty + W$, where the correction $W$ is smooth near $r_0$ and solves, for all $w$,
$$
\int_\Omega \sigma \nabla W \cdot \nabla w = \int_\Omega (\sigma_\infty - \sigma)\, \nabla V_\infty \cdot \nabla w \; - \oint_{\partial\Omega} \sigma_\infty\, \partial_n V_\infty \; w \, dS .
$$
*Derivation*: apply Green's identity to $V_\infty$ on $\Omega$, then subtract it from the weak form of $V$. The volume integrand vanishes near $r_0$, so every right-hand side is regular.
:::

### 2.4 Lead field and reciprocity

::: def
[Definition 2.7 — Lead field]{.tag} Column $j$ of the lead field $G$ is the forward solution for a unit dipole at source $j$, sampled at the electrodes. With the average reference it becomes
$$
G \leftarrow H G, \qquad H = I_m - \tfrac{1}{m} \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top .
$$
For MEG, the field is then computed from $V$ by Biot–Savart; the Geselowitz formula of section 9.1 does this with surface integrals.
:::

Computing $G$ column by column takes one solve per source, that is $10^4$ solves for a cortical source space. Reciprocity reverses the roles of sources and sensors.

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.8 — Helmholtz reciprocity]{.tag} Let $U_{ab}$ be the potential created when a current $I$ is injected at electrode $a$ and extracted at electrode $b$:
$$
\nabla \cdot (\sigma \nabla U_{ab}) = 0 \ \text{ in } \Omega, \qquad \sigma\, \partial_n U_{ab} = I\, (\delta_a - \delta_b) \ \text{ on } \partial\Omega .
$$
Then, for every primary current $J^p$,
$$
V(a) - V(b) = \frac{1}{I} \int_\Omega J^p \cdot \nabla U_{ab}\, dr, \qquad \text{and for a dipole} \qquad V(a) - V(b) = \frac{q \cdot \nabla U_{ab}(r_0)}{I} .
$$

::: proof
Apply Green's identity (Theorem 0.2) to the pair $(V, U_{ab})$ in both orders.

*First order.* Since $\nabla\cdot(\sigma\nabla U_{ab}) = 0$,
$$
\int_\Omega \sigma \nabla V \cdot \nabla U_{ab} = \oint V\, \sigma\, \partial_n U_{ab} = I\,\big(V(a) - V(b)\big) .
$$

*Second order.* Since $\sigma\,\partial_n V = 0$ on the boundary,
$$
\int_\Omega \sigma \nabla U_{ab} \cdot \nabla V = -\int_\Omega U_{ab}\, \nabla \cdot J^p = \int_\Omega J^p \cdot \nabla U_{ab} ,
$$
the last step by parts, $J^p$ vanishing on the boundary. Equating the two expressions gives the result. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

One solve per electrode (relative to the reference) thus gives every row of $G$. The discrete version is exact: since $K$ is symmetric, $(e_a - e_b)^\top K^{+} b = b^\top K^{+} (e_a - e_b)$, which is the identity of Theorem 2.8 for the FEM solution.

::: ex
[Code 2.9 — P1 finite elements on a disk: direct versus subtraction source model, and reciprocity]{.tag} The 2D unit disk with $\sigma = 1$ has an exact solution by the method of images: the Neumann function is $N(r, s) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\big(\ln|r - s| + \ln|r - s^*|\big)$ with $s^* = s/|s|^2$, and $V = -q \cdot \nabla_s N(r, s)$ at $s = r_0$.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial import Delaunay
from scipy.sparse import coo_matrix
from scipy.sparse.linalg import spsolve

def disk_mesh(n_rings):
    """Nodes on concentric rings of the unit disk; the last ring is the scalp."""
    pts = [np.zeros((1, 2))]
    for k in range(1, n_rings + 1):
        t = 2 * np.pi * np.arange(6 * k) / (6 * k)
        pts.append(k / n_rings * np.c_[np.cos(t), np.sin(t)])
    p = np.vstack(pts)
    return p, Delaunay(p).simplices, np.arange(len(p) - 6 * n_rings, len(p))

def stiffness(p, tri, sigma=1.0):
    """P1 stiffness matrix and the gradients of the hat functions per triangle."""
    M = np.concatenate([np.ones((len(tri), 3, 1)), p[tri]], axis=2)
    G = np.linalg.inv(M)[:, 1:, :].transpose(0, 2, 1)       # (T, 3, 2)
    area = np.abs(np.linalg.det(M)) / 2
    Ke = sigma * area[:, None, None] * G @ G.transpose(0, 2, 1)
    I, J = np.repeat(tri, 3, axis=1).ravel(), np.tile(tri, (1, 3)).ravel()
    return coo_matrix((Ke.ravel(), (I, J)), shape=(len(p),) * 2).tocsr(), G

def solve_neumann(K, b):
    """Ground node 0 (V is defined up to a constant), then remove the mean."""
    K = K.tolil(); K[0, :] = 0; K[0, 0] = 1; b = b.copy(); b[0] = 0
    v = spsolve(K.tocsr(), b)
    return v - v.mean()

def v_inf(x, r0, q):                       # 2-D infinite-medium dipole, sigma = 1
    d = x - r0
    return (d @ q) / (2 * np.pi * np.sum(d**2, axis=1))

def grad_v_inf(x, r0, q):
    d = x - r0; d2 = np.sum(d**2, axis=1)[:, None]
    return (q / d2 - 2 * (d @ q)[:, None] * d / d2**2) / (2 * np.pi)

def rhs_direct(p, tri, G, r0, q):          # b_i = q . grad phi_i(r0)
    t = Delaunay(p).find_simplex(r0)
    b = np.zeros(len(p)); b[tri[t]] = G[t] @ q
    return b

def rhs_subtraction(p, bd, r0, q):         # b_i = - int dV_inf/dn phi_i ds
    b, (gx, gw) = np.zeros(len(p)), np.polynomial.legendre.leggauss(3)
    s, w = (gx + 1) / 2, gw / 2
    for i, j in zip(bd, np.roll(bd, -1)):
        e = p[j] - p[i]; L = np.linalg.norm(e); n = np.array([e[1], -e[0]]) / L
        flux = grad_v_inf(p[i] + s[:, None] * e, r0, q) @ n
        b[i] -= L * np.sum(w * flux * (1 - s)); b[j] -= L * np.sum(w * flux * s)
    return b

def exact(x, r0, q, h=1e-6):               # image solution in the unit disk
    def N(s):
        return (np.log(np.linalg.norm(x - s, axis=1))
                + np.log(np.linalg.norm(x - s / (s @ s), axis=1))) / (2 * np.pi)
    v = -sum(qk * (N(r0 + h * e) - N(r0 - h * e)) / (2 * h)
             for qk, e in zip(q, np.eye(2)))
    return v - v.mean()

r0, q = np.array([0.3, 0.2]), np.array([1.0, 0.5])
for n in [10, 20, 40, 80]:
    p, tri, bd = disk_mesh(n)
    K, G = stiffness(p, tri)
    va = exact(p[bd], r0, q)
    v1 = solve_neumann(K, rhs_direct(p, tri, G, r0, q))
    v2 = solve_neumann(K, rhs_subtraction(p, bd, r0, q)) + v_inf(p, r0, q)
    err = [np.linalg.norm(v[bd] - v[bd].mean() - va) / np.linalg.norm(va) for v in (v1, v2)]
    print(f"rings {n:2d}, h = {1/n:.4f}: direct {err[0]:.1e}, subtraction {err[1]:.1e}")

a, b = bd[0], bd[len(bd) // 4]             # reciprocity on the finest mesh
inj = np.zeros(len(p)); inj[a], inj[b] = 1.0, -1.0
U = solve_neumann(K, inj)                  # unit current injected at a, out at b
t = Delaunay(p).find_simplex(r0)
print(f"V(a) - V(b) = {v1[a] - v1[b]:.6f}, q . grad U(r0) = {q @ (G[t].T @ U[tri[t]]):.6f}")
```

Output: the relative error of the scalp potential falls from $9.7 \times 10^{-4}$ to $1.5 \times 10^{-5}$ with the subtraction model, a factor of about 4 per halving of $h$. The direct model stalls between $3 \times 10^{-3}$ and $4 \times 10^{-2}$, depending on where the dipole falls inside its triangle. Both sides of the reciprocity identity print 0.311940.
:::

Boundary element methods, which mesh only the interfaces, are the main alternative for nested homogeneous compartments (section 9.1). Finite elements handle anisotropy, holes in the skull and arbitrary geometry, at the price of a volume mesh built from a segmented MRI.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 2
:::

-   The EEG forward problem is a Neumann problem for $\nabla\cdot(\sigma\nabla V) = \nabla\cdot J^p$; its solution is unique up to a constant.
-   The weak form is well posed for $L^2$ sources (Lax–Milgram); P1 finite elements give the energy-optimal approximation (Céa).
-   A point dipole is singular: the subtraction approach restores the $h^2$ convergence that the direct approach loses.
-   Reciprocity gives each row of the lead field from one solve with current injected at a pair of electrodes.
::::

## 3. Preprocessing and denoising M/EEG signals {#ch3}

A raw recording mixes brain activity of interest with eye blinks, heartbeats, muscle activity, line noise and ongoing background activity, often larger than the signal sought. This chapter gives the linear tools that separate them, and states the assumptions each one makes.

### 3.1 Signal model and sources of noise

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Measurement model]{.tag} Over $T$ time samples, the data matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times T}$ is modelled as
$$
X = G S + A + N,
$$
where $G S$ is the activity of interest, $A$ the artifacts (ocular, cardiac, muscular, movement, 50 Hz line noise and its harmonics), and $N$ the sensor noise and background brain activity, spatially correlated.
:::

### 3.2 Filtering and averaging

A band-pass filter keeps the band of interest (1–40 Hz for evoked responses, 8–30 Hz for sensorimotor rhythms) and a notch removes the line frequency. Offline, zero-phase filtering avoids delays; online, as in a BCI, filters must be causal.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — Averaging over trials]{.tag} Let epochs time-locked to a stimulus be $x_k(t) = s(t) + n_k(t)$, $k = 1, \dots, N$, with a response $s$ identical across trials and noises $n_k$ independent, centred and of variance $\sigma^2$. The average $\bar x$ satisfies
$$
\mathbb{E}\,\bar x(t) = s(t), \qquad \mathrm{Var}\, \bar x(t) = \frac{\sigma^2}{N} ,
$$
so the amplitude signal-to-noise ratio grows as $\sqrt N$.

::: proof
Linearity of expectation gives the mean. The noises are independent, so the variance of their sum is $N\sigma^2$, divided by $N^2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 3.3 — How many trials?]{.tag} An evoked component of 2 µV in background activity of standard deviation 10 µV has a single-trial SNR of 0.2. Reaching an SNR of 3 requires $\sqrt N \ge 15$:
$$
N \ge 225 \text{ trials}.
$$
If the latency jitters from trial to trial, the average is the response convolved with the jitter distribution, smaller and wider than $s$.
:::

### 3.3 Noise covariance and whitening

:::: def
[Definition 3.4 — Whitening]{.tag} Let $C_N = \mathbb{E}[n n^\top]$ be the noise covariance across sensors, estimated on a baseline or on an empty-room recording, and regularised when few samples are available. The whitener is
$$
W = C_N^{-1/2}, \qquad \tilde X = W X = (W G)\, S + W N, \qquad \mathrm{Cov}(W n) = I_m .
$$

::: proof
Since $C_N^{-1/2}$ is symmetric,
$$
\mathrm{Cov}(Wn) = W C_N W^\top = C_N^{-1/2} C_N C_N^{-1/2} = I .
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Whitening puts channels of different units (EEG in volts, magnetometers and gradiometers in teslas and teslas per metre) on a common scale. Least squares on whitened data is generalised least squares, the efficient estimator under correlated noise (Proposition 5.3 states the same fact for fMRI).

### 3.4 Signal-space projection

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.5 — Signal-space projection (SSP; Uusitalo and Ilmoniemi, 1997)]{.tag} Let the columns of $U_a \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times k}$ be an orthonormal basis of the artifact topographies, estimated by a PCA of artifact epochs (blinks, heartbeats) or of empty-room data. The matrix
$$
P = I_m - U_a U_a^\top
$$
is the orthogonal projector onto the complement of $\mathrm{span}(U_a)$. Then $P A = 0$ for every artifact whose topographies lie in $\mathrm{span}(U_a)$, and the projected data obey $P X = (P G) S + P N$.

::: proof
$P$ is symmetric and $P^2 = I - 2U_aU_a^\top + U_a (U_a^\top U_a) U_a^\top = P$, since $U_a^\top U_a = I_k$. If $A = U_a C$, then $PA = U_a C - U_a C = 0$. The last identity is linearity. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Two consequences matter in practice. The lead field must be projected as well ($PG$), otherwise source estimates are biased. And the component of every brain topography along $U_a$ is lost: a source whose topography resembles a blink is attenuated with it.

### 3.5 Independent component analysis

::: def
[Definition 3.6 — ICA model]{.tag} The data are an instantaneous mixture $x(t) = A\, s(t)$ of $k$ sources, with $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times k}$ of rank $k$ and source components that are mutually independent, centred and of unit variance. ICA seeks an unmixing matrix $B$ with
$$
B x = P D\, s ,
$$
for some permutation $P$ and diagonal $D$: order and scale are not identifiable.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 3.7 — Identifiability (Comon, 1994)]{.tag} If at most one source is Gaussian, the mixing matrix is identifiable up to permutation and scaling of its columns. With two or more Gaussian sources, any rotation of them is again a valid solution. The proof rests on the Darmois–Skitovich theorem.
:::

After PCA whitening, $z = W x$ has identity covariance and $z = Q s$ with $Q$ orthogonal, since $Q Q^\top = \mathrm{Cov}(z) = I$. It remains to find a rotation, which non-Gaussianity determines.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.8 — Kurtosis as a contrast]{.tag} Let $\kappa_i$ be the fourth cumulant (excess kurtosis) of $s_i$, assumed positive for all $i$. For a unit vector $w$, set $u = Q^\top w$ (also a unit vector), so that $y = w^\top z = u^\top s$. Then
$$
\kappa(y) = \sum_i u_i^4 \kappa_i ,
$$
and the maximum over the unit sphere is attained at $u = \pm e_{i^*}$ with $i^* = \arg\max_i \kappa_i$: the output is then one of the sources.

::: proof
Fourth cumulants add over independent variables and scale with the fourth power, which gives the formula.

Since $|u_i| \le 1$, $u_i^4 \le u_i^2$, so
$$
\sum_i u_i^4 \kappa_i \le \max_i \kappa_i \sum_i u_i^2 = \kappa_{i^*},
$$
with equality at $u = \pm e_{i^*}$. Each $\pm e_i$ is moreover a local maximum, and Delfosse and Loubaton (1995) show that there are no others. Deflation then extracts the sources one by one. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

FastICA (Hyvärinen and Oja, 2000) maximises an approximation of negentropy with a nonlinearity $g$ and the fixed-point update, followed by normalisation,
$$
w \leftarrow \mathbb{E}[z\, g(w^\top z)] - \mathbb{E}[g'(w^\top z)]\, w .
$$
Components that correlate with an EOG or ECG channel, or look like blinks, are zeroed before back-projection.

::: ex
[Code 3.9 — Removing blinks by SSP and by ICA]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import FastICA
from scipy.stats import kurtosis

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
fs, T = 250, 20                                   # 250 Hz, 20 s
t = np.arange(fs * T) / fs
alpha = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * t) * (1 + 0.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 0.2 * t))
beta = rng.standard_normal(t.size)                # broadband background source
blink = np.zeros_like(t)
for t0 in rng.uniform(0.5, T - 0.5, size=12):     # 12 blinks, about 0.3 s each
    blink += 8 * np.exp(-0.5 * ((t - t0) / 0.06) ** 2)
S = np.vstack([alpha, beta, blink])               # (3 sources, time)

n_ch = 8
A = rng.standard_normal((n_ch, 3))
A[:, 2] = np.abs(A[:, 2]) * np.linspace(2, 0.2, n_ch)   # blink: frontal channels
X_brain = A[:, :2] @ S[:2]
X = X_brain + np.outer(A[:, 2], blink) + 0.1 * rng.standard_normal((n_ch, t.size))

def report(name, Xc):
    D = Xc - X_brain
    D -= D.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)            # offsets are removed by high-pass filtering
    err = np.linalg.norm(D) / np.linalg.norm(X_brain)
    print(f"{name:22s} relative error to the artifact-free signal: {err:.3f}")

report("raw", X)

# Signal-space projection: first principal direction of the blink periods
mask = blink > 1.0
U, _, _ = np.linalg.svd(X[:, mask] - X[:, mask].mean(1, keepdims=True), full_matrices=False)
u = U[:, :1]
P = np.eye(n_ch) - u @ u.T                        # projector onto the complement
report("SSP (1 component)", P @ X)

# ICA: the blink component is the one with the largest kurtosis
ica = FastICA(n_components=3, whiten="unit-variance", random_state=0, max_iter=1000)
Sh = ica.fit_transform(X.T)                       # (time, components)
k = np.argmax(kurtosis(Sh, axis=0))
Sh[:, k] = 0
report("ICA (blink removed)", ica.inverse_transform(Sh).T)
print("kurtosis of the components:", np.round(kurtosis(ica.transform(X.T), axis=0), 1))
print("angle between blink topography and SSP vector (deg):",
      round(np.degrees(np.arccos(abs(u[:, 0] @ A[:, 2]) / np.linalg.norm(A[:, 2]))), 2))
```

Output: the relative error drops from 2.655 (raw) to 0.388 with SSP and 0.060 with ICA. The SSP vector is within 2.3° of the blink topography, yet SSP also removes the brain signal along it (Proposition 3.5). ICA isolates the blink (kurtosis 11.8).
:::

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 3
:::

-   Averaging $N$ time-locked trials divides the noise standard deviation by $\sqrt N$, if the response is identical across trials and the noise independent.
-   Whitening by $C_N^{-1/2}$ equalises sensor types and turns least squares into generalised least squares.
-   SSP removes a subspace of topographies exactly, together with the brain signal in that subspace; the lead field must be projected too.
-   ICA separates independent non-Gaussian sources up to order and scale; artifacts are removed by zeroing their components.
::::

## 4. The M/EEG inverse problem {#ch4}

Given the measurements and the lead field, where are the active sources? The problem is ill-posed, and every method adds an assumption: few dipoles, uncorrelated sources, or a prior on the amplitudes. This chapter covers MUSIC, beamforming and imaging, and their validation.

### 4.1 Ill-posedness

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.1 — Non-uniqueness and instability]{.tag} Let $M = G J + N$ with $G \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times p}$ and $p > m$.

1.  The kernel of $G$ has dimension at least $p - m$: adding any $J_0 \in \ker G$ (a *silent source*) leaves the data unchanged.
2.  With the SVD $G = \sum_i s_i u_i v_i^\top$, the minimum-norm least-squares solution is $G^+ M = \sum_{s_i > 0} \frac{u_i^\top M}{s_i}\, v_i$, so noise along $u_i$ is amplified by $1/s_i$.

::: proof
Item 1 is the rank–nullity theorem, since $\mathrm{rank}\, G \le m$. Item 2 is Definition 0.4. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Helmholtz (1853) already noted that currents inside a conductor cannot be recovered from external measurements; radial dipoles in MEG (Theorem 1.9) are an explicit silent source. The singular values of a realistic lead field decay over several orders of magnitude, so regularisation is unavoidable.

### 4.2 Dipole fitting

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — Variable projection]{.tag} For $k$ dipoles at positions $\mathbf r = (r_1, \dots, r_k)$, with lead field $G(\mathbf r) \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times 3k}$ and moments $Q \in \mathbb{R}^{3k \times T}$,
$$
\min_{Q} \|M - G(\mathbf r)\, Q\|_F^2 = \big\| \big(I - G(\mathbf r) G(\mathbf r)^+\big) M \big\|_F^2 ,
$$
attained at $Q = G(\mathbf r)^+ M$. The fit reduces to a nonlinear problem in $3k$ position parameters.

::: proof
For fixed positions the problem is linear least squares, column by column; its solution is $G^+ M$ and the residual is the projection of $M$ onto the orthogonal complement of the range of $G(\mathbf r)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The reduced cost has local minima and is minimised from a grid of starting points. The *goodness of fit* $1 - \|P^\perp M\|^2/\|M\|^2$ is the explained variance. Dipole fitting suits focal responses, such as early auditory components.

### 4.3 MUSIC

Assume $k$ sources with fixed positions, topographies $G_S = [g_1, \dots, g_k]$ and time courses of covariance $C_Q$, in white noise (after whitening). The data covariance is
$$
R = G_S C_Q G_S^\top + \sigma^2 I_m .
$$

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.3 — MUSIC (Schmidt, 1986; Mosher, Lewis and Leahy, 1992)]{.tag} Let $G_S$ have full column rank $k$ and $C_Q$ be positive definite. Let $U_s$ be the eigenvectors of $R$ with the $k$ largest eigenvalues.

For a candidate topography $g(r)$, the subspace correlation
$$
c(r) = \frac{\|U_s^\top g(r)\|^2}{\|g(r)\|^2} \in [0, 1]
$$
equals 1 exactly when $g(r) \in \mathrm{span}(G_S)$; in particular $c(r_j) = 1$ at every true source.

::: proof
The matrix $G_S C_Q G_S^\top$ has range $\mathrm{span}(G_S)$. It is contained in it. Conversely, for $x = G_S y$, choose $z$ with $G_S^\top z = C_Q^{-1} y$, which is possible since $G_S^\top$ has full row rank; then
$$
G_S C_Q G_S^\top z = G_S y = x .
$$

Its non-zero eigenvalues are positive and its eigenvectors span this range. Adding $\sigma^2 I$ shifts all eigenvalues by $\sigma^2$, so the top $k$ eigenvectors of $R$ span $\mathrm{span}(G_S)$.

Finally $c(r)$ is the squared cosine between $g(r)$ and this subspace, equal to 1 if and only if $g(r)$ lies in it. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

In practice $R$ is estimated and $c$ peaks near, not exactly at, the sources. RAP-MUSIC (Mosher and Leahy, 1999) projects out each source found before scanning again, which avoids picking secondary peaks of the same source. If two sources are perfectly correlated, $C_Q$ is singular and the theorem fails.

### 4.4 Beamforming

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.4 — LCMV beamformer (Van Veen et al., 1997)]{.tag} Let $C$ be the data covariance, positive definite. The spatial filter that passes a source at $r$ with unit gain and minimises the output power,
$$
\min_{w}\ w^\top C w \quad \text{subject to} \quad w^\top g(r) = 1,
$$
is
$$
w(r) = \frac{C^{-1} g(r)}{g(r)^\top C^{-1} g(r)}, \qquad \text{with output power} \qquad P(r) = \frac{1}{g(r)^\top C^{-1} g(r)} .
$$

::: proof
The Lagrangian $w^\top C w - 2\mu\,(w^\top g - 1)$ has gradient $2Cw - 2\mu g$, which vanishes at $w = \mu C^{-1} g$. The constraint gives $\mu = 1/(g^\top C^{-1} g)$. The objective is strictly convex, so this point is the minimum, and $w^\top C w = \mu^2\, g^\top C^{-1} g = \mu$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.5 — A single source is recovered with its power]{.tag} If $C = P\, g_0 g_0^\top + C_N$ (one source of power $P$ plus noise), then at the true location
$$
P(r_0) = P + \frac{1}{g_0^\top C_N^{-1} g_0} .
$$

::: proof
Set $\alpha = g_0^\top C_N^{-1} g_0$. By the Sherman–Morrison formula,
$$
g_0^\top C^{-1} g_0 = \alpha - \frac{P \alpha^2}{1 + P\alpha} = \frac{\alpha}{1 + P\alpha} ,
$$
whose inverse is $P + 1/\alpha$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The noise term $1/\alpha$ grows with depth, because deep sources have small topographies. The *neural activity index* divides $P(r)$ by $1/(g^\top C_N^{-1} g)$ to remove it. Beamformers assume uncorrelated sources: two perfectly correlated sources cancel each other (Exercise 10).

### 4.5 Distributed imaging: minimum-norm estimates

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.6 — Minimum-norm estimate as a posterior mean (Hämäläinen and Ilmoniemi, 1994)]{.tag} Let $M = G J + N$ with $N \sim \mathcal{N}(0, C_N)$ and the prior $J \sim \mathcal{N}(0, R/\lambda)$, $R$ positive definite. The posterior mean of $J$, which is also the minimiser of
$$
\|M - G J\|^2_{C_N^{-1}} + \lambda\, J^\top R^{-1} J ,
$$
is the linear estimate

::: key
[Key result — the minimum-norm inverse operator]{.tag}
$$
\hat J = W M, \qquad W = R\, G^\top \big(G R G^\top + \lambda\, C_N\big)^{-1}
$$
:::

::: proof
$(J, M)$ is jointly Gaussian with $\mathrm{Cov}(J, M) = R G^\top/\lambda$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(M) = G R G^\top/\lambda + C_N$. The conditional mean is $\mathrm{Cov}(J, M)\,\mathrm{Cov}(M)^{-1} M$, which gives $W$ after multiplying inside and outside by $\lambda$.

For a Gaussian posterior the mean is also the mode, hence the minimiser of the negative log-posterior, which is the displayed objective up to constants. Equivalently, change variables to $\tilde J = R^{-1/2} J$ and $\tilde M = C_N^{-1/2} M$, and apply Proposition 0.5. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

With $R = I$, the estimate favours superficial sources, whose topographies have a large norm. *Depth weighting* uses $R = \mathrm{diag}(\|g_j\|^{-2\gamma})$ with $\gamma$ between 0.5 and 0.8. The regularisation $\lambda$ is often set to $1/\mathrm{SNR}^2$ on whitened data.

::: def
[Definition 4.7 — dSPM and sLORETA]{.tag} Take $R = I$ and write $T = (G G^\top + \lambda C_N)^{-1}$, so that $W = G^\top T$. Two normalisations of $\hat J_j$ are standard:

-   **dSPM** (Dale et al., 2000) divides by the noise standard deviation of the estimate: $z_j = \hat J_j / \sqrt{(W C_N W^\top)_{jj}}$.
-   **sLORETA** (Pascual-Marqui, 2002) divides by the standard deviation under the full model (source plus noise), which equals the diagonal of the resolution matrix $W G$:
    $$
    s_j = \frac{\hat J_j^2}{(W G)_{jj}}, \qquad \text{since} \quad W (G G^\top + \lambda C_N) W^\top = G^\top T G = W G .
    $$
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.8 — sLORETA localises a single source without bias]{.tag} With fixed orientations, noise-free data $M = g_k\, a$ from one source $k$ of amplitude $a \neq 0$, and any $\lambda > 0$, the sLORETA map is maximal at the true source:
$$
s_j \le s_k \quad \text{for all } j, \qquad \text{with equality only if } g_j \text{ is collinear with } g_k .
$$

::: proof
$T$ is symmetric positive definite, so $\langle x, y \rangle_T = x^\top T y$ is an inner product. The estimate is $\hat J_j = g_j^\top T g_k\, a$ and $(W G)_{jj} = \langle g_j, g_j \rangle_T$, hence
$$
s_j = \frac{\langle g_j, g_k\rangle_T^2}{\langle g_j, g_j\rangle_T}\, a^2 \le \langle g_k, g_k \rangle_T\, a^2 = s_k
$$
by Cauchy–Schwarz, with equality only for collinear vectors. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The theorem says nothing about several simultaneous sources or about noise, where sLORETA can be biased; the unnormalised MNE is biased even in this ideal case. Sparse priors (minimum current or mixed-norm estimates) are treated in section 9.2.

### 4.6 Validation

::: def
[Definition 4.9 — Resolution matrix, point spread and cross-talk]{.tag} For a linear inverse operator $W$, $\hat J = W G J + W N$. The **resolution matrix** is $\mathcal R = W G \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}$.

-   Column $k$ is the **point-spread function** of source $k$: how a unit source at $k$ is spread over the estimate.
-   Row $j$ is the **cross-talk function** of location $j$: how all sources leak into the estimate at $j$.
-   The **localisation error** of source $k$ is the distance from $k$ to the peak of its point-spread function. With $d_{jk}$ the distance between locations, the **spatial dispersion** is
    $$
    \mathrm{SD}_k = \Big(\sum_j d_{jk}^2 \mathcal R_{jk}^2 \Big/ \sum_j \mathcal R_{jk}^2\Big)^{1/2} .
    $$
:::

For MNE with $R = I$, $\mathcal R = G^\top T G$ is symmetric: point-spread and cross-talk functions coincide. Validation also uses simulations at realistic SNR, phantoms, known functional anatomy, intracranial recordings or fMRI of the same task, and test–retest reliability.

::: ex
[Code 4.10 — Localisation error of five inverse methods on a toy EEG model]{.tag} The forward model is Proposition 1.5 (infinite homogeneous medium), with radial dipoles on two shells at 7 cm (superficial) and 5 cm (deep), and 60 electrodes at 9 cm.

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

def fib_sphere(n, radius, zmin=0.0):
    """Quasi-uniform points on the upper part (z > zmin) of a sphere."""
    k = np.arange(n) + 0.5
    z = 1 - k / n * (1 - zmin)
    phi = np.pi * (1 + 5**0.5) * k
    rho = np.sqrt(1 - z**2)
    return radius * np.c_[rho * np.cos(phi), rho * np.sin(phi), z]

# Sources: radial dipoles on two shells (superficial 7 cm, deep 5 cm); 60 EEG electrodes at 9 cm
src = np.vstack([fib_sphere(300, 0.07, 0.2), fib_sphere(150, 0.05, 0.2)])
ori = src / np.linalg.norm(src, axis=1, keepdims=True)
elec = fib_sphere(60, 0.09, 0.0)
sigma = 0.33
d = elec[:, None, :] - src[None, :, :]                       # (60, 450, 3)
G = np.einsum("ijk,jk->ij", d, ori) / (4 * np.pi * sigma * np.linalg.norm(d, axis=2) ** 3)
H = np.eye(60) - 1 / 60                                      # average reference
G = H @ G                                                     # V/(A m)

def simulate(k, snr=1.0, n_t=200):
    s = 10e-9 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * np.arange(n_t) / 1000)   # 10 nAm, 10 Hz
    M0 = np.outer(G[:, k], s)
    noise_sd = np.linalg.norm(M0) / np.sqrt(M0.size) / snr
    return M0 + H @ (noise_sd * rng.standard_normal(M0.shape)), noise_sd**2 * H

def localise(M, Cn, lam=1 / 9):
    Cn_r = Cn + 1e-6 * np.trace(Cn) / 60 * np.eye(60)        # regularised noise covariance
    T = np.linalg.inv(G @ G.T + lam * np.trace(G @ G.T) / np.trace(Cn_r) * Cn_r)
    W = G.T @ T                                               # minimum-norm operator
    J = W @ M
    p_mne = np.sum(J**2, axis=1)
    p_dspm = p_mne / np.einsum("ij,jk,ik->i", W, Cn_r, W)     # noise-normalised
    p_slor = p_mne / np.einsum("ij,ji->i", W, G)              # diag of the resolution matrix
    C = M @ M.T / M.shape[1] + 0.05 * np.trace(M @ M.T) / M.shape[1] / 60 * np.eye(60)
    Ci = np.linalg.inv(C)
    p_lcmv = 1 / np.einsum("ij,jk,ki->i", G.T, Ci, G)         # unit-gain beamformer power
    p_lcmv /= np.einsum("ij,jk,ki->i", G.T, np.linalg.inv(Cn_r), G) ** -1  # neural activity index
    U = np.linalg.svd(M, full_matrices=False)[0][:, :1]       # signal subspace, rank 1
    p_music = np.sum((U.T @ G) ** 2, axis=0) / np.sum(G**2, axis=0)
    return {name: np.argmax(p) for name, p in
            [("MNE", p_mne), ("dSPM", p_dspm), ("sLORETA", p_slor),
             ("LCMV", p_lcmv), ("MUSIC", p_music)]}

for depth, ks in [("superficial", range(0, 300, 30)), ("deep", range(300, 450, 15))]:
    errs = {}
    for k in ks:
        M, Cn = simulate(k)
        for name, j in localise(M, Cn).items():
            errs.setdefault(name, []).append(1000 * np.linalg.norm(src[j] - src[k]))
    print(f"{depth:11s} mean localisation error (mm): " +
          ", ".join(f"{n} {np.mean(e):5.1f}" for n, e in errs.items()))
```

Output, in mm: superficial sources, MNE 6.9, dSPM 12.4, sLORETA, LCMV and MUSIC 0.0; deep sources, MNE 40.4, dSPM 3.9, the others 0.0. The depth bias of MNE is plain; at an SNR of 0.1 all methods degrade.
:::

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 4
:::

-   The inverse problem has silent sources and small singular values: every method adds an assumption.
-   Dipole fitting reduces to a nonlinear problem in the positions (variable projection); MUSIC scans the signal subspace; LCMV filters with unit gain and minimum power.
-   The minimum-norm estimate is the posterior mean under Gaussian priors; dSPM and sLORETA normalise it, and sLORETA has no localisation bias for one noise-free source.
-   The resolution matrix $WG$ summarises a linear method; simulations, phantoms and known anatomy validate it.
::::

## 5. fMRI: the BOLD signal and the general linear model {#ch5}

In which of the hundred thousand voxels of an fMRI run does the signal follow the task, and is the effect present in the population, not only in the subjects scanned? The general linear model and its two-level extension answer.

### 5.1 The BOLD signal

Deoxyhaemoglobin is paramagnetic and oxyhaemoglobin is not. When a brain area becomes active, blood flow increases more than oxygen consumption, so the local concentration of deoxyhaemoglobin falls. The field inhomogeneities it creates decrease, the transverse relaxation time $T_2^*$ lengthens, and the MR signal rises by 1–5 % at 3 T: the **BOLD** contrast (Ogawa et al., 1990).

The response is slow: it peaks about 5 s after a brief stimulus, then undershoots. It correlates best with local field potentials, hence with synaptic activity (Logothetis et al., 2001). A volume of 2–3 mm voxels is acquired every 1–2 s (the repetition time, TR), corrected for motion, registered to a template and often smoothed.

### 5.2 The linear model of the response

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Haemodynamic response and design matrix]{.tag} The BOLD response is modelled as a linear time-invariant system (Friston et al., 1994): for experimental conditions with onset functions $u_c$,
$$
y(t) = \sum_c \beta_c\, (h * u_c)(t) + d(t) + \varepsilon(t),
$$
with the canonical **haemodynamic response function** (HRF), a difference of two gamma densities, time in seconds:
$$
h(t) = \frac{t^5 e^{-t}}{5!} - \frac{1}{6}\, \frac{t^{15} e^{-t}}{15!} ,
$$
which peaks at 5 s and has its undershoot near 16 s. Sampling at the $n$ scan times gives $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$. The columns of the **design matrix** $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ are the convolved regressors, a low-frequency drift basis $d$ (cosines of period above about 128 s) and a constant.
:::

Linearity holds well for stimuli a few seconds apart; closer stimuli saturate, which nonlinear models such as the balloon model describe (Buxton et al., 1998). Adding the time derivative of $h$ to the design absorbs small shifts of latency.

### 5.3 Estimation and inference

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.2 — $t$ and $F$ tests of contrasts]{.tag} Assume $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I_n)$ and $\mathrm{rank}\, X = p$; let $c \in \mathbb{R}^p$ and $C \in \mathbb{R}^{q \times p}$ of rank $q$.

Under $H_0: c^\top \beta = 0$, respectively $H_0: C\beta = 0$,
$$
t = \frac{c^\top \hat\beta}{\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2\, c^\top (X^\top X)^{-1} c}} \sim t_{n-p}, \qquad F = \frac{(C\hat\beta)^\top \big[C (X^\top X)^{-1} C^\top\big]^{-1} C\hat\beta}{q\, \hat\sigma^2} \sim F_{q,\, n-p} .
$$

::: proof
By Theorem 0.7, under $H_0$,
$$
c^\top\hat\beta \sim \mathcal{N}\big(0, \sigma^2 c^\top(X^\top X)^{-1}c\big),
$$
independently of $(n-p)\hat\sigma^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-p}$. The ratio of a standard normal to the square root of an independent $\chi^2_{n-p}/(n-p)$ is $t_{n-p}$.

For $F$, the quadratic form in the numerator is $\sigma^2 \chi^2_q$ under $H_0$, since $C\hat\beta$ is Gaussian with covariance $\sigma^2 C (X^\top X)^{-1} C^\top$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.3 — Prewhitening]{.tag} If $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 V)$ with $V$ known and positive definite, let $W$ satisfy $W V W^\top = I$. Then $W y = (W X)\beta + W\varepsilon$ has white errors, and least squares on the whitened model is the generalised least-squares estimate
$$
\hat\beta_{\mathrm{GLS}} = (X^\top V^{-1} X)^{-1} X^\top V^{-1} y ,
$$
the best linear unbiased estimate; Theorem 5.2 applies to $(Wy, WX)$.

::: proof
The whitened errors have covariance $\sigma^2 W V W^\top = \sigma^2 I$, and $W^\top W = V^{-1}$, which turns the OLS formula into the GLS formula. Optimality is the Gauss–Markov theorem in the whitened coordinates. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

fMRI noise is autocorrelated; an AR(1) model with coefficient $\rho$ has a bidiagonal whitener, with first row $\sqrt{1-\rho^2}$, then rows $(-\rho, 1)$. Ignoring the autocorrelation inflates false positives (Code 5.6). The **efficiency** of a design for $c$ is $1/\big(c^\top (X^\top X)^{-1} c\big)$: blocks of 15–20 s maximise it; jittered events estimate the response shape better.

### 5.4 Mixed-effects models for group analysis

::: def
[Definition 5.4 — Two-level model]{.tag} For subjects $s = 1, \dots, S$, the first level gives an estimate $\hat\beta_s$ of the subject's effect, with known variance $v_s$; the second level models the subjects as a sample of the population:
$$
\hat\beta_s = \beta_s + e_s, \quad e_s \sim \mathcal{N}(0, v_s), \qquad \beta_s = \mu + \eta_s, \quad \eta_s \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2) ,
$$
so that marginally $\hat\beta_s \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, v_s + \tau^2)$. A **fixed-effects** analysis sets $\tau^2 = 0$ and concerns only the subjects scanned; a **random-effects** (mixed-effects) analysis concerns the population.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.5 — Weighted mean and the summary-statistics test]{.tag} For known variances, the maximum-likelihood estimate of $\mu$ is the precision-weighted mean
$$
\hat\mu = \frac{\sum_s w_s \hat\beta_s}{\sum_s w_s}, \qquad w_s = \frac{1}{v_s + \tau^2}, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu) = \frac{1}{\sum_s w_s} .
$$
If all $v_s$ are equal, $\hat\mu$ is the plain mean. The one-sample $t$ test on the subject estimates is then exact with $S - 1$ degrees of freedom, without estimating $\tau^2$ or the $v_s$.

::: proof
The log-likelihood is $-\frac12 \sum_s w_s(\hat\beta_s - \mu)^2$ up to constants, maximised at the weighted mean; its variance is $\sum_s w_s^2 (v_s + \tau^2)/(\sum_s w_s)^2 = 1/\sum_s w_s$. In the balanced case the $\hat\beta_s$ are i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(\mu, v + \tau^2)$, the setting of the one-sample $t$ test. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

This *summary-statistics* approach (Holmes and Friston, 1998) is robust when within-subject variances are similar. In general, the linear mixed model $y = X\beta + Z b + \varepsilon$, with $b \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Gamma)$, has covariance $V = Z \Gamma Z^\top + \sigma^2 I$; its fixed effects follow by GLS (Proposition 5.3), its variance components by restricted maximum likelihood.

::: ex
[Code 5.6 — First-level GLM with AR(1) noise, and fixed versus random effects]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import gamma, t as student

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
TR, n = 2.0, 200                                   # 200 scans, 6 min 40 s

def hrf(tt):                                       # canonical double-gamma (SPM shape)
    return gamma.pdf(tt, 6) - gamma.pdf(tt, 16) / 6

dt = 0.1
tt = np.arange(0, 32, dt)
u = (np.arange(0, n * TR, dt) % 40 < 20).astype(float)   # 20 s on / 20 s off
reg = np.convolve(u, hrf(tt))[: u.size] * dt
reg = reg[:: int(TR / dt)]                         # sample at the scan times
k = np.arange(1, 5)                                # discrete cosine drifts, period > 128 s
time = np.arange(n) * TR
drift = np.cos(np.pi * np.outer(time / (n * TR), k))
X = np.column_stack([reg, drift, np.ones(n)])
c = np.r_[1.0, np.zeros(X.shape[1] - 1)]           # contrast: effect of the task

def ar1_noise(rho, sd, size):
    e = np.zeros(size)
    e[0] = rng.normal(0, sd / np.sqrt(1 - rho**2))
    for i in range(1, size):
        e[i] = rho * e[i - 1] + rng.normal(0, sd)
    return e

def glm_t(y, X, rho=0.0):
    """OLS (rho = 0) or GLS after AR(1) prewhitening with a known rho."""
    W = np.eye(len(y)) - rho * np.eye(len(y), k=-1)
    W[0, 0] = np.sqrt(1 - rho**2)
    Xw, yw = W @ X, W @ y
    beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(Xw, yw, rcond=None)
    res = yw - Xw @ beta
    dof = len(y) - X.shape[1]
    s2 = res @ res / dof
    var_c = s2 * c @ np.linalg.inv(Xw.T @ Xw) @ c
    return c @ beta, (c @ beta) / np.sqrt(var_c), dof

# One voxel: 1% signal change on a baseline of 100, AR(1) noise with rho = 0.4
y = 100 + 1.0 * reg / reg.max() + 0.5 * drift[:, 0] + ar1_noise(0.4, 0.8, n)
for name, rho in [("OLS", 0.0), ("GLS, AR(1)", 0.4)]:
    b, tval, dof = glm_t(y, X, rho)
    print(f"{name:11s} beta = {b:.3f}, t = {tval:.2f}, p = {student.sf(tval, dof):.1e}")

# False-positive rate of OLS under AR(1) noise and no activation (nominal 5 %)
fp = [np.mean([glm_t(100 + ar1_noise(0.4, 0.8, n), X, r)[1] > student.isf(0.05, n - X.shape[1])
               for _ in range(500)]) for r in (0.0, 0.4)]
print(f"null voxels declared active at p < 0.05: OLS {fp[0]:.3f}, GLS {fp[1]:.3f}")

# Group: 12 subjects, true mean effect 0.4, between-subject sd 0.5
betas, var_b = [], []
for s in range(12):
    effect = 0.4 + 0.5 * rng.standard_normal()
    ys = 100 + effect * reg / reg.max() + ar1_noise(0.4, 0.8, n)
    b, tval, dof = glm_t(ys, X, 0.4)
    betas.append(b); var_b.append((b / tval) ** 2)
betas, var_b = np.array(betas), np.array(var_b)
t_fixed = betas.sum() / np.sqrt(var_b.sum())       # ignores between-subject variance
t_random = betas.mean() / (betas.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(12))
print(f"group: fixed-effects t = {t_fixed:.2f}, random-effects t = {t_random:.2f} "
      f"(p = {student.sf(t_random, 11):.3f}, 11 dof)")
```

Output: OLS gives $t = 8.00$ and GLS $t = 5.39$ for the same voxel. On 500 null voxels, OLS declares 11.8 % active at the nominal 5 %, GLS 5.6 %. At the group level, the fixed-effects $t$ is 6.14 and the random-effects $t$ is 2.55 ($p = 0.014$): only the second supports a claim about the population.
:::

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 5
:::

-   BOLD is a slow, indirect marker of synaptic activity: the HRF peaks about 5 s after the event.
-   The GLM convolves the experimental conditions with the HRF; contrasts are tested with $t$ and $F$ statistics (Theorem 5.2).
-   Autocorrelated noise must be prewhitened, otherwise false positives inflate.
-   Population inference needs the between-subject variance: two-level mixed-effects models, or the summary-statistics $t$ test when the design is balanced.
::::

## 6. Hypothesis testing and multiple comparisons {#ch6}

A statistical map tests one hypothesis per voxel, or per sensor and time point: tens of thousands of tests at once. This chapter makes precise which error rate is controlled, and gives tests that remain valid without distributional assumptions.

### 6.1 Mass-univariate testing

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Familywise error and false discovery rates]{.tag} Among $V$ tests, let $V_0$ be the true nulls, $R$ the number of rejections and $F$ the number of false rejections. The **familywise error rate** and the **false discovery rate** are
$$
\mathrm{FWER} = P(F \ge 1), \qquad \mathrm{FDR} = \mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{F}{\max(R, 1)}\Big] .
$$
:::

At an uncorrected threshold of $p < 0.001$, a map of 50 000 voxels under the global null contains 50 false positives on average: the dead salmon of the introduction.

### 6.2 Permutation tests

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.2 — Exactness of permutation tests]{.tag} Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a finite group of $B$ transformations of the data (relabellings, or sign flips) that leave the distribution of the data $X$ invariant under $H_0$. For a statistic $T$, define
$$
p(X) = \frac{1}{B}\, \#\{g \in \mathcal{G} : T(gX) \ge T(X)\} .
$$
Then $P(p(X) \le \alpha) \le \alpha$ under $H_0$ for every $\alpha \in [0, 1]$.

::: proof
Let $g'$ be uniform on $\mathcal{G}$, independent of $X$. Under $H_0$, $g'X$ has the law of $X$, so
$$
P(p(X) \le \alpha) = P(p(g'X) \le \alpha) .
$$

The orbit $\{g g' X : g \in \mathcal G\}$ equals $\{gX\}$, since the transformations form a group. Hence $p(g'X)$ is the rank, from the top, of $T(g'X)$ among the values of the orbit, divided by their number.

Given the orbit, at most $\alpha B$ of its elements have a rank of at most $\alpha B$, and $g'$ picks one uniformly. So the conditional probability is at most $\alpha$, and so is its expectation. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For a group analysis, the subject effect maps are symmetric around zero under $H_0$, so flipping their signs leaves the distribution invariant: $2^S$ transformations (Nichols and Holmes, 2002). When $B$ is too large, a random sample of $B - 1$ transformations plus the identity keeps the test valid.

### 6.3 Controlling the familywise error rate

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.3 — Bonferroni and the maximum statistic]{.tag}

1.  Rejecting the tests with $p_v \le \alpha / V$ gives $\mathrm{FWER} \le \alpha$.
2.  Let $u_\alpha$ be the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of the permutation distribution of $\max_v T_v$. Rejecting the tests with $T_v > u_\alpha$ controls the FWER at level $\alpha$ under the global null.

::: proof
1.  By the union bound over the set $\mathcal{V}_0$ of true nulls,
    $$
    P(F \ge 1) \le \sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}_0} P(p_v \le \alpha/V) \le \frac{V_0\, \alpha}{V} \le \alpha .
    $$
2.  Under the global null, a false rejection occurs exactly when $\max_v T_v > u_\alpha$, an event of probability at most $\alpha$ by Theorem 6.2 applied to the statistic $\max_v T_v$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The maximum statistic adapts to the correlation between tests: on a smooth map it gives a lower threshold than Bonferroni. Control extends to any configuration of true nulls under the *subset pivotality* condition (Westfall and Young, 1993). Random field theory is the parametric alternative (section 9.3).

### 6.4 The false discovery rate

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.4 — Benjamini–Hochberg procedure (1995)]{.tag} Sort the p-values $p_{(1)} \le \dots \le p_{(V)}$, let $k = \max\{i : p_{(i)} \le q\, i / V\}$, and reject the $k$ smallest. If the null p-values are uniform and independent of each other and of the non-null ones,
$$
\mathrm{FDR} = \frac{V_0}{V}\, q \le q .
$$

::: proof
For a null test $v$, let $R_0^{(v)}$ be the number of rejections when $p_v$ is replaced by 0; it depends only on the other p-values.

The step-up rule gives the equality of events
$$
\{v \text{ rejected}, R = k\} = \{p_v \le qk/V,\ R_0^{(v)} = k\}:
$$
a rejected $p_v$ can be lowered to 0 without changing the rejections, and conversely.

By independence, $P(v \text{ rejected}, R = k) = \frac{qk}{V} P(R_0^{(v)} = k)$. Hence
$$
\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{\mathbb{1}\{v \text{ rejected}\}}{\max(R,1)}\Big] = \sum_{k=1}^V \frac{1}{k}\, \frac{qk}{V}\, P(R_0^{(v)} = k) = \frac{q}{V},
$$
and summing over the $V_0$ null tests gives the result. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The bound also holds under positive regression dependence (Benjamini and Yekutieli, 2001), a reasonable model for smooth maps. FDR is an average: on a given map the proportion of false discoveries can exceed $q$.

### 6.5 Cluster-level inference

::: def
[Definition 6.5 — Cluster inference]{.tag} Threshold the map at a cluster-forming level $u$ (for instance $p < 0.001$), form the connected components of supra-threshold voxels, and measure each by its size or mass (sum of statistics). Comparing each cluster with the permutation distribution of the *largest* cluster controls the FWER at the cluster level.
:::

A significant cluster means that at least one of its voxels is active. The result depends on $u$, which threshold-free cluster enhancement avoids (Smith and Nichols, 2009). Eklund et al. (2016) found parametric cluster inference invalid at liberal thresholds, and permutation valid. For M/EEG, clusters span sensors, times and frequencies (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007).

::: ex
[Code 6.6 — Uncorrected, Bonferroni, maximum-statistic and FDR thresholds on a smooth map]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter
from scipy.stats import t as student

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
```
